newsitem.title: USA: Glickman sees big battle over gene-modified crops.
newsitem.headline: Glickman sees big battle over gene-modified crops.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman warned Tuesday that the United States could find itself in a major dispute with the European Union and other trading partners over the safety of genetically modified crops.
"This is really shaping up to be the battle royale of 21st century world agriculture," Glickman said in a speech to the Washington Commodity Club, a group of agricultural industry lobbyists.

A growing portion of U.S. corn, soybean and other crop production comes from seed varieties that have been genetically modified to produce higher yields. In many cases, the genetically modified crops require less water and other agricultural inputs than traditional crops.

However, many consumers, especially in Europe, have strong concerns about the safety of genetically modified crops and would like to see them kept separate from traditional crops throughout the marketing chain. That would make it much easier for food processors to label whether their products contain genetically modified ingredients or not.

The U.S. grain industry is strongly opposed to segregation because of the huge costs involved. They also argue the action is unnecessary because the crops are not a threat to human health, a view upheld by the U.S. government.

In his speech, Glickman repeated that the United States "will not tolerate" any requirement to segregate genetically modified crops and said the United States would go to the World Trade Organisation to prevent that from happening.
But hectoring the European Union on the unfair trade aspects of segragation is "a losing argument," Glickman said.
The United States must convince opponents that genetically modified crops and other biotechnology innovations are needed to feed "a growing world in a sustainable way," he said.
